title: 舊唐書 198, the Fu-lin account — Byzantium described from the Tang court, with the water-cooled roof, the golden hour-scale, and four embassies between 643 and 719
language_note:
THIS RECORD CARRIES NO SOURCE-LANGUAGE TEXT AND THE `language_code` SAYS SO. The tier is `published_translation_only` and the only text on the record is English. The Literary Chinese of the Jiu Tangshu is not transcribed here, was not captured, and is not claimed.

AND `original_text_excerpt` IS OMITTED RATHER THAN FILLED WITH A PLACEHOLDER, which raises the loader warning `empty original_text_excerpt, no original chunk emitted`. The warning is the honest artefact. `africa-01-ezana-stone` is what the alternative costs six weeks later: a bracketed note saying the source text is to be pulled during ingestion classifies as a `pointer`, suppresses nothing, and reads to a later session as though the work were half done. FINDING 80.

THE CORPUS ALREADY HOLDS THE CHINESE OF FOUR OTHER FU-LIN AND DA-QIN ACCOUNTS — `eastasia-01-weilue`, `eastasia-02-hou-hanshu`, `eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun`, `eastasia-06-cefu-yuangui`, `eastasia-07-tang-huiyao` and `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin`. This one is deliberately the English-only member of that family, because the tier needs a record that is nothing but a published translation and its citation.
date: The Jiu Tangshu was compiled in the mid-10th century CE and covers 618–906 CE; the events in this passage run from the reign of Yang-ti of the Sui (605–617) to an embassy of 719. All of it sits inside the project's window, and the 719 embassy is the latest datable event in any East Asian record in this corpus except `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin`.
reference_translation:
The country of Fu-lin [Byzantium], also called Ta-ts'in [Roman Syria], lies above the western sea [Indian Ocean]. In the southeast it borders on Po-si [Persia]. Its territory amounts to over 10,000 li. Of cities there are four hundred. Inhabited places are close together. The eaves, pillars, and window-bars of their palaces are frequently made with crystal and opaque glass. There are twelve honorable ministers who conjointly regulate government matters. They ordinarily let a man take a bag and follow the king's carriage. When the people have a complaint they throw a written statement into the bag. When the king comes back to the palace he decides between right and wrong. Their kings are not permanent rulers, but they select men of merit. If an extraordinary calamity visits the country, or if wind and rain come at the wrong time, he is deposed and another man is put in his stead. The king's cap is shaped like a bird raising its wings; its trimmings are beset with precious pearls; he wears silk-embroidered clothing, without a lapel in front. He sits on a throne with golden ornaments. He has a bird like a goose; its feathers are green, and it always sits on a cushion by the side of the king. Whenever anything poisonous has been put into the king's meals, the bird will crow. The walls of their capital are built of granite, and are of enormous height [the Theodosian triple walls]. The city[Constantinople] contains in all over 100,000 households [some 500,000 to 600,000 inhabitants]. In the south it faces the great sea. In the east of the city there is a large gate; its height is over twenty chang [over 235 feet]; it is beset with yellow gold [bronze] from top to bottom, and shines at a distance of several li. Coming from outside to the royal residence there are three large gates beset with all kinds of rare and precious stones. On the upper floor of the second gate they have suspended a large golden scale, twelve golden balls are suspended from the scale-stick by which the twelve hours of the day are shown. A human figure has been made all of gold of the size of a man standing upright, on whose side, whenever an hour has come, one of the golden balls will drop, the dingling sound of which makes known the divisions of the day without the slightest mistake [a clepsydra]. In the palaces, pillars are made of se-se [lapis lazuli], the floors of yellow gold [probably bronze], the leaves of folding doors of ivory, beams of fragrant wood. They have no tiles, but powdered plaster is rammed down into a floor above the house. This floor is perfectly firm and of glossy appearance like jade-stone. When, during the height of summer, the inhabitants are oppressed by heat, they lead water up and make it flow over the platform, spreading it all over the roof by a secret contrivance so that one sees and knows not how it is done, but simply hears the noise of a well on the roof; suddenly you see streams of water rushing down from the four eaves like a cataract; the draught caused thereby produces a cooling wind, which is due to this skilful contrivance [a common device in the Near East].

It is customary for men to have their hair cut and wear robes leaving the right arm bare. Women have no lapels on their dresses, they wear turbans of embroidered cloth. The possession of a great fortune confers superior rank on its owner. There are lambs which grow in the ground; the inhabitants wait till they are about to sprout, and then screen them off by building walls to prevent the beasts which are at large outside from eating them up. The navel of these lambs is connected with the ground; when it is forcibly cut the animal will die, but after the people have fixed the buds themselves' they frighten them by the steps of horses or the beating of drums, when the lambs will yield a sound of alarm, and the navel will be detached, and then the animal may be separated from the water-plant. The inhabitants are in the habit of cutting their hair and wearing embroidered clothing; they drive in small carriages with white canopies; when going in or out they beat drums and hoist flags, banners, and pennants. The country contains much gold, silver, and rare gems. There is the Yeh-kuang-pi [the jewel that shines at night]; the ming-yüeh-chu [the moon-shine pearl]; the hsieh-chi-hsi [the chicken-frightening rhinoceros stone]; large conches; the che-ch'u [mother-of-pearl], carnelian stones; the k'ung-ts'ui [Jadeite]; corals; amber; and all the valuable curiosities of the West are exported from this country.

The emperor Yang-ti of the Sui dynasty [605-617 C.E.] always wished to open intercourse with Fu-lin, but did not succeed. In the 17th year of the period Cheng-kuan [643 C.E.], the king of Fu-lin Po-to-li [Constans II Pogonatus, Emperor 641-668 C.E.] sent an embassy offering red glass, lu-chin-ching [green gold gems], and other articles. T'ai-tsung [the then ruling emperor] favored them with a message under his imperial seal and graciously granted presents of silk. Since the Ta-shih [the Arabs] had conquered these countries they sent their commander-in-chief, Mo-i [Mo'awiya], to besiege their capital city; by means of an agreement they obtained friendly relations, and asked to be allowed to pay every year tribute of gold and silk; in the sequel they became subject to Ta-shih. In the second year of the period Ch'ien-feng [667 C.E.] they sent an embassy offering Ti-yeh-ka. In the first year of the period Ta-tsu [701 C.E.] they again sent an embassy to our court. In the first month of the seventh year of the period K'ai-yuan [719 C.E.] their lord sent the ta-shou-ling [an officer of high rank] of T'u-huo-lo [Khazarstan] to offer lions and ling-yang[antelopes], two of each. A few months after, he further sent ta-te-seng ["priests of great virtue"] to our court with tribute.

VERIFIED BY DIGEST ACROSS TWO MACHINES. The span is Hirth's lettered extract K as the Internet East Asian History Sourcebook prints it, from the first word of the translation to the last, WITHOUT the Sourcebook's own header line — `From the Chiu-t'ang-shu, ch. 198 (written mid-10th Century C.E.), for 618-906 C.E.:` — which is the page's furniture and is itself a rewriting of Hirth's bracketed heading. Sliced in the browser between that header and the header of the next extract; typed on the bridge in seven pieces and joined; SHA-256 computed on both machines over the result.

**THE LARGEST EXCERPT IN THIS CORPUS**, more than twice `africa-07-cosmas-sasu`'s 2,777, and it is taken whole because extract K is one continuous translated passage and cutting it anywhere would be this project choosing which parts of a Tang historian's account of Byzantium matter.

CHECKED FOR WHAT A READER CANNOT SEE: exactly one non-ASCII character in 5,833 — a `ü` at index 4265, in `ming-yüeh-chu` — four newlines, forming two paragraph breaks, and no double space anywhere.

EVERY ODDITY IN IT IS THE SOURCE'S AND NONE IS REPAIRED. `The city[Constantinople]` and `ling-yang[antelopes]` have no space before the bracket. `after the people have fixed the buds themselves' they frighten them` carries a stray apostrophe. `skilful` is spelled the British way in an American sourcebook. All of it stands.
translation_source:
F. Hirth, `China and the Roman Orient: Researches into their Ancient and Mediaeval Relations as Represented in Old Chinese Records` (Leipsic & Munich: Georg Hirth; Shanghai & Hong Kong: Kelly & Walsh, 1885), lettered extract **K**, printed pp. 51–56 — **as modified by Jerome S. Arkenberg for the Internet East Asian History Sourcebook, 2000**, and read off https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/romchin1.html on 2026-09-06. The page states its own source line: `From: F. Hirth, China and the Roman Orient: Researches into their Ancient and Mediaeval Relations as Represented in Old Chinese Records (Shanghai & Hong Kong, 1885), pp. 35-96.` and, separately, `The text has been modified by Dr. Arkenberg. [Any modernization © 2000 Jerome S. Arkenberg.]`

THE BOUNDARY OF THE TRANSLATION SEARCH, WHICH THIS TIER OWES, AND IT IS A COMPARISON RATHER THAN A LIST OF PLACES LOOKED AT.

WHAT WAS OPENED: the Sourcebook page, and Hirth 1885 itself in the Internet Archive scan `chinaandromanor00hirtgoog` (metadata `possible-copyright-status: NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT`; the DLI copy `in.ernet.dli.2015.24269` carries `Rights: In Public Domain`). Extract K begins on printed page 51, immediately after the running header `TRANSLATIONS: I-K. 51`, which was read in this session.

WHAT THE COMPARISON FOUND, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING. Hirth's own text opens `[1] The country of Fu-lin, also called Ta-ts'in, lies above the western sea. [2] In the south-east it borders on Po-ssu [Persia].` The Sourcebook's opens `The country of Fu-lin [Byzantium], also called Ta-ts'in [Roman Syria], lies above the western sea [Indian Ocean]. In the southeast it borders on Po-si [Persia].` So the modernization (a) DELETES Hirth's numbered sentences, which are how the whole of `China and the Roman Orient` is cross-referenced; (b) RESPELLS a transliteration, `Po-ssu` to `Po-si`; and (c) ADDS bracketed identifications where Hirth has none. `[Persia]` is Hirth's. `[Byzantium]`, `[Roman Syria]` and `[Indian Ocean]` are not.

AND FOUR OF THE IDENTIFICATIONS IN THIS EXCERPT DO NOT OCCUR ANYWHERE IN HIRTH 1885 AT ALL. Searched in the scan's full text on 2026-09-06: `Theodosian` — absent; `Pogonatus` — absent; `Khazarstan` — absent; `Mo'awiya` at that spelling — absent. `clepsydra` occurs in the volume, roughly ninety thousand characters after extract K ends, in Hirth's apparatus rather than in his translation. **So `[the Theodosian triple walls]`, `[Constans II Pogonatus, Emperor 641-668 C.E.]`, `[Khazarstan]` and `[a clepsydra]` are the modernizer's identifications standing inside the translated text in the same brackets Hirth uses for his own.**

WHAT THIS RECORD THEREFORE CLAIMS AND DOES NOT CLAIM. It claims to hold the Sourcebook's electronic text of Hirth's extract K, verbatim and digest-verified, with the translator, the modernizer and the difference between them named. **It does NOT claim to hold Hirth 1885 as printed.** A reader who needs Hirth's own wording has the scan, the page range and the nature of the differences.

WHAT WAS NOT OPENED: no later English translation of the Jiu Tangshu Fu-lin chapter was searched for beyond Hirth, and none is claimed to be absent. The Chinese text was not captured, so nothing here rests on it.

WHY BOTH, AND WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin`'S CELL ON THE SAME URL. That record's cell quotes the first statement and not the second, and it was right to for what it was doing: the Sourcebook supplied one half of a bilingual record whose Chinese came from Kanripo. **On this record the modernization IS the text.** The second statement asserts copyright over precisely the thing this record carries, with no grant attached, while the first grants educational and personal copying over the electronic form and refuses commercial use. Neither is adjudicated here. The source is credited by name, which is the one thing the first statement actually asks for.

NOBODY RE-CURATES A RECORD, so `eastasia-08`'s cell stands as it is. This one is not a correction of it; it is a different question asked of the same page.
notes:
F7's East Asia `published_translation_only` slot. Sixth record of the tranche, fifty-third in the corpus, and the FIRST OF THE TWO RECORDS THAT CLOSE THAT TIER.

WHAT IT SAYS. A Tang-dynasty history describing Byzantium: four hundred cities; twelve ministers who govern jointly; a king who is deposed if the rains come at the wrong time; a bag carried behind the royal carriage for written complaints; granite walls of enormous height; a gate of bronze twenty chang high; a golden scale on the second gate from which twelve golden balls drop to mark the hours; roofs cooled in summer by water led up and released over the eaves; and the lambs that grow in the ground and must be frightened loose from their navels. Then the embassies: Yang-ti of the Sui wished to open intercourse and failed; in 643 the king of Fu-lin sent red glass and green gold-gems; the Arabs besieged the capital and were bought off with annual tribute of gold and silk; and further embassies came in 667, 701 and 719, the last bringing lions and antelopes and, months later, `priests of great virtue`.

THE CORPUS'S THIRD FU-LIN RECORD AND ITS FOURTH ACCOUNT OF THE 643 EMBASSY. `eastasia-06-cefu-yuangui` and `eastasia-07-tang-huiyao` hold Fu-lin in Literary Chinese; `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin` holds the Song History's account four hundred years later. THIS IS DELIBERATE AND IT IS RULING 79's P1. F6 discovered that the Song History's account of 拂菻 crowded the Cefu Yuangui's account of 拂菻 — same subject, four centuries apart, and the older record lost two ranks. This is a third account of the same subject in English, and P1 predicts `cefu-yuangui-fulin-glass` falls again with chunks of this record in its `beaten_by`. That prediction was written before this file existed.

WHY THIS EXTRACT AND NOT HIRTH'S L OR I. Extract L is the Xin Tangshu's Fu-lin chapter, which partly rewrites this one; extract I is the Wei shu on Ta-ts'in, which is largely derivative of the Hou Hanshu the corpus already holds. Both were readable on the same page and both were refused, because there is one East Asia slot and extract K is the one that carries the embassies.

WHAT THE TIER GAINS, AND IT IS NOT ONLY A COUNT. `published_translation_only` stood at 2 of 4 and its two members were `africa-01-ezana-stone` — a placeholder whose translation is a titulature quoted from a news website — and `africa-07-cosmas-sasu`, a public-domain scholarly translation with a named translator, publisher and page range. **This is the tier's first record that is a text OF one of the seven regions rather than a Roman-world author writing about one.** The corpus's Africa members are both Rome looking outward; this is East Asia looking at Rome, in English because the tier is about translations and not about scripts.

AND THE MODERNIZATION QUESTION IS THE RECORD'S REAL CONTRIBUTION. `translation_source` records what a comparison against Hirth's own scan found: deleted sentence numbers, a respelled transliteration, and at least four identifications — Theodosian, Pogonatus, Khazarstan, clepsydra — that do not appear in Hirth 1885 and now sit inside the translation in Hirth's own bracket style. **This corpus has cited this page before without knowing that**, on `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin`, and the finding is not retroactive because nobody re-curates a record. What it changes is what a later block may say about any text taken from a sourcebook that describes itself as modified.

ONE OF THOSE IDENTIFICATIONS IS ALSO A CLAIM THIS RECORD DECLINES TO ADOPT. `T'u-huo-lo [Khazarstan]` — the bracket is the modernizer's and this record imports no gazetteer id on the strength of it, exactly as it imports none for `their capital city [Constantinople]`. Taking a place id off a modernizer's bracket would be authoring a coordinate through a third party.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE. F7 holds one declaration, Block F's last, and it is spent on `persia-07-met-ewer-anahita`. This is the fourth F7 record with declarable material and no declaration.

subject_places.name: Fu-lin (Ta-ts'in) — the country the passage is organised around
subject_places.note: NO ID. `Fu-lin` and `Ta-ts'in` name a state and its people as a Tang historian understood them, and this corpus has refused a gazetteer id for `kēsar`, `Hrōmāy`, `walhakurn`, `mlk Rmn`, `mlk Frs¹` and `ngs²yn` on the rule that a people, a state, an office and a title are not settlements. Pleiades 423025 `Roma` is emphatically not imported here: the passage is about a polity whose capital it describes as facing the great sea, which is not Rome.

subject_places.name: Their capital city — walls of granite, a bronze gate twenty chang high, and the golden hour-scale
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE INTERESTING ONE. The translation reads `The city[Constantinople] contains in all over 100,000 households` — but `[Constantinople]` is the MODERNIZER'S bracket and not Hirth's, and the underlying text names no city at all. Importing a Pleiades id for Constantinople on the strength of a 2000 editorial gloss would be authoring a coordinate through a third party, which is the same refusal `NEVER AUTHOR A COORDINATE` makes directly. Recorded as a waypoint because the embassies pass through it and the Arab siege arrives at it; recorded without an id because the source this record holds does not name it.

subject_places.name: Our court — the Tang court the embassies are sent to
subject_places.note: NO ID. The text says `they again sent an embassy to our court`, in the voice of a Chinese history, and names no city. The Tang capital is not stated and is not supplied. The role is `destination` because four embassies travel to it across the passage, which is the movement the record exists to document.

subject_places.name: Ta-shih — the Arabs, who besiege the capital and take annual tribute of gold and silk
subject_places.note: NO ID. `Ta-shih` is a people, refused an id on the standing rule. The role is `destination` because something moves to them and it is stated: `asked to be allowed to pay every year tribute of gold and silk; in the sequel they became subject to Ta-shih`. This is the corpus's first record of the Roman world paying tribute rather than receiving embassies.

subject_places.name: Po-si — Persia, which the passage puts on Fu-lin's southeastern border
subject_places.note: NO ID, and `mentioned` rather than a directional role because nothing moves along that border in this passage: it is a fact of geography as a Tang historian states it. `[Persia]` is one of the few brackets here that IS Hirth's own. Hirth spells the transliteration `Po-ssu`; the electronic text this record holds spells it `Po-si`, which is one of the modernizations named in `translation_source`.

subject_places.name: T'u-huo-lo — where the officer who brought the lions and antelopes in 719 came from
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND A GLOSS THIS RECORD DECLINES TO ADOPT. The electronic text reads `the ta-shou-ling [an officer of high rank] of T'u-huo-lo [Khazarstan]`. `Khazarstan` appears nowhere in Hirth 1885 and is the modernizer's identification. This record takes no position on what T'u-huo-lo denotes and imports no id on the strength of a bracket added in 2000.
